clue.text: Green, the company -wrecker — what a fool!

definitions.meaning: an unripe-looking green fruit of a thorny bush
an unwanted third person who spoils a couple's time together
a fool is a creamy pudding, often made with this fruit

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at a foolish person who wrecked a business while still green.
explanation.walkthrough: Three senses: the green fruit, the person who 'plays' it by spoiling a couple's company, and the fruit fool, a British dessert of puréed fruit and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit is green, playing it means intruding on a pair, and a fool is a classic pudding made from it.

clue.text: Charlemagne's favourite biscuit?

definitions.meaning: one of the emperor's paladins, friend of Roland
the Bath kind, a dry savoury biscuit

explanation.surface: Asking which biscuit the emperor Charlemagne liked best.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bath Oliver is a British plain biscuit eaten with cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous paladin of the Frankish emperor, and a plain cheese cracker named after a Bath doctor.

clue.text: Skill of the captain, or his ship

explanation.surface: Praising a captain's expertise, or else his vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamanship is maritime skill; a seagoing vessel is also so called.

clue.text: A risky business, but no one is quick, to kick its wares

definitions.text: no one is quick, to kick its wares
definitions.meaning: a shop selling pails, and nobody hurries to 'kick the bucket', i.e. die

explanation.surface: A dodgy firm whose goods nobody is in a hurry to kick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kick the bucket' is slang for die, so no one rushes to kick what such a shop sells.
explanation.definitionFit: A dubious stockbroker or cut-price travel agent, and literally a store for pails.

clue.text: Gets it back from the one named in 21

definitions.text: Gets it back from the one named in 21

parts.words: Gets it back from the one named in 21
parts.note: 21's 'uncle' is slang for a pawnbroker, from whom pledged goods are recovered

explanation.surface: Someone retrieves an item from their uncle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is old British slang for a pawnbroker; pawned goods are bought back.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying back a pledged item from a pawnbroker.

clue.text: 24 in the old old days

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: ye is an archaic form of 'the'
the answer to 24 is the metal, and or is heraldic gold

explanation.surface: Gold as it was in bygone times.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 refers to the solution of 24-down; heraldry calls that metal OR.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic term for times long past.

clue.text: Fiery love-bird?.

parts.note: flaming means fiery
love is zero in tennis, O

explanation.surface: A passionate lovebird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love-bird' looks like one word; it splits into O and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pink wading bird with long legs, whose colour suits 'fiery'.

clue.text: Once fashionable in the outskirts of Victoria

definitions.text: Once fashionable in the outskirts of Victoria

parts.words: Once fashionable in the outskirts of Victoria
parts.note: not suburbs of a city but the wide hooped skirts of the Victorian era

explanation.surface: Something formerly stylish in the suburbs of Victoria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outskirts' suggests city fringes; read it as skirts worn outermost in Queen Victoria's day.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooped petticoats that held out the wide skirts fashionable in the Victorian period.

clue.text: Employee at the Coach and Horses

definitions.text: Employee at the Coach and Horses

parts.words: Employee at the Coach and Horses
parts.note: read literally, a worker at an inn who tends the horses that pull the coaches, not a pub barman

explanation.surface: A worker at a pub called the Coach and Horses.
explanation.walkthrough: The Coach and Horses is a common British pub name; an old inn's stableman looked after travellers' horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A stableman at a coaching inn, caring for travellers' horses.

clue.text: Put up money for a propeller and retaining civil engineer

parts.note: a fish's fin propels it through water

indicators.note: one word holds the abbreviation inside it, as a container keeps something

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone funded an aircraft propeller and kept on a civil engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retaining' puts CE inside AND, giving ANCED after FIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To fund something is to put up the money for it.

clue.text: He may never represent popular morality

indicators.note: the letters re-present themselves in a new order

parts.note: fodder for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A man who may never stand for the morals of the people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represent' is read as re-present, a rearranging of MAY NEVER. The definition is the famous medieval morality play.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval morality play, widely performed, whose title character stands for all humanity.

clue.text: Made for a Malayan boatman

parts.note: a craft built for a sailor in the Malay seas; also PRO (for) plus A reads within it

explanation.surface: Something constructed for a Malayan sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: A swift outrigger sailing craft of the Malay archipelago; 'for a' also gives PRO + A.
explanation.definitionFit: A Malay outrigger sailing vessel, the kind of craft a Malayan sailor would use.

clue.text: Love is confused with pity, to be sure

indicators.note: the letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: fodder for the rearrangement
fodder for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone mixes up love with pity, certainly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic ways of saying certainly.

clue.text: This broadcast gives us the pip

definitions.text: This broadcast gives us the pip

parts.words: This broadcast gives us the pip
parts.note: the radio pips that mark the hour, not the depressing 'pip' that annoys us

explanation.surface: A broadcast that annoys listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'give someone the pip' is British slang for annoying them; the BBC's six pips mark the exact hour.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC's hourly pips are a radio marker of the exact hour.

clue.text: Plenty to eat, but will it go round?

definitions.text: Plenty to eat, but will it go round?

parts.words: Plenty to eat, but will it go round?
parts.note: a hearty meal, with the wordplay asking whether something square can be round

explanation.surface: Worrying whether a big spread will feed everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go round' means suffice, but also plays against the 'square' of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A substantial, satisfying meal.

clue.text: Incomplete, like Dickens's pseudonymous works?

definitions.meaning: Dickens wrote Sketches by Boz under the pen name Boz

explanation.surface: A remark that some of Dickens's pen-name writing feels unfinished.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough and lacking detail; and resembling Dickens's early pieces published as Sketches by Boz.

clue.text: Sort of act giving power to serve up poison fish?

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the word is read upwards

parts.note: bane is a poison
ling is a fish

explanation.surface: Serving poisoned fish as an act of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'serve up' turns BANE into ENAB.
explanation.definitionFit: An Act of Parliament granting powers is called this kind of act.

clue.text: "Take a letter"—trust M Dupin to find it!

definitions.text: Take a letter"—trust M Dupin to find it

parts.words: Take a letter"—trust M Dupin to find it
parts.note: to take a letter by stealth, as in Poe's story where the detective Dupin recovers a stolen letter

explanation.surface: A boss dictates a letter, trusting the famous detective to track it down.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Purloined Letter' has C. Auguste Dupin find a stolen letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To steal is to take; Poe's detective finds a stolen letter.

clue.text: Solicitor transferred by Libs to the corridors of power?

indicators.note: the letters are moved around into a new order

parts.note: fodder for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A lawyer moved by the Liberals to Westminster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' looks like a lawyer; it means one who solicits votes from legislators in the corridors of power.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who seeks to influence politicians, soliciting their support.

clue.text: Sailor Jack madly embraced by a sea goddess

indicators.note: one piece is held inside another

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the letters go crazy and change order

parts.note: a jack tar is a sailor, TAR

explanation.surface: A sailor clasped by a sea goddess in a frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' turns TAR into TRA, which 'embraced by' sets inside SEA after A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek star-maiden deity of justice.

clue.text: Change of key man

parts.note: not a reshuffle of important staff but a musician who shifts a piece into another key

explanation.surface: A reshuffle of an important employee.
explanation.definitionFit: A musician or device that moves music into a different key.

clue.text: Your uncle's named as OK for bell-ringing exercises .

definitions.meaning: '... your uncle' is a British phrase meaning all is well
change-ringing sequences in which bells swap places

explanation.surface: An uncle's approval of some practice on the church bells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob's your uncle' is everyday British for 'and there you are'.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase name, and a term for particular change-ringing methods in campanology.

clue.text: Gas, only one in Scotland?

parts.note: but means only, as in 'but a child'
ane is Scots for one

explanation.surface: Asking whether Scotland has only one gas.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrocarbon fuel stored in canisters for lighters and stoves.

clue.text: Countryman has a drink after 6.50

indicators.note: the drink is placed following the two numerals

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
L is fifty in Roman numerals
lager is a drink, a light beer

explanation.surface: A rural man has a beer after ten to seven in the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 6.50 looks like a time of day; it is read as Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A rural inhabitant living in a small settlement.

clue.text: Standard brick swindle

definitions.meaning: a monetary standard backed by the precious metal
a ... brick is a fake ingot used to con people

explanation.surface: A conventional fraud involving bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: A currency standard and, in a gold brick, a confidence trick.

clue.text: Statesman in a cream outfit?

indicators.note: to outfit is to fit out, here a reworking of the letters

parts.note: fodder for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A politician wearing a cream suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Statesman' means not a politician but a man from the States.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the United States, punningly a States-man.

clue.text: It's over the door, to allow none to return

indicators.note: both words are turned round and read from right to left

parts.note: to let is to allow
nil means none

explanation.surface: Something above a door that refuses re-entry to anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' reverses LET + NIL as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A horizontal beam spanning the top of a doorway.

clue.text: Law is ineffective when the landlord's late

definitions.meaning: a statute still on the books but no longer enforced
a letter (one who lets property) who has died

explanation.surface: Legal powers count for nothing once the landlord has died.
explanation.walkthrough: A landlord is one who lets, so a dead landlord is a dead 'letter'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rule no longer observed; and punningly a deceased person who lets property.
